Torah, Draft and the Kaplan Standard

In Israel 2026, every riot now comes with the same customer‑service question: “Would this have happened on Kaplan?”

On one side, the establishment Haredi world plays by appointment. Hamodia, the Gur‑aligned daily, leads with arrests of draft deserters and summons thousands of Hasidim for a 16:00 protest outside Military Prison 10 — a fully coordinated event with police, branded as “with prayers and without public disorder.” 

On the other, the hardline Jerusalem Faction disciples block the Geha Interchange and Route 4 at rush hour, until a commander declares an illegal demonstration and stun grenades, batons and even ripped‑off pants turn Bnei Brak asphalt into a live‑fire test of police standards.

The political class immediately calibrates it against the secular protests that once filled Kaplan Street. Yair Lapid goes for the jugular: Aryeh Deri, he says, sits in the security cabinet sending “our kids” to fight and die, then walks outside and sends “his kids” to block roads against the draft, all with the tacit blessing of Netanyahu, Smotrich and Ben Gvir — “a moral stain this government will never wash off.” 

In his framing, the double game is the whole story: coalition leaders cash in on state sovereignty and coalition budgets, then franchise out civil disobedience when the same state dares to demand service from their own base.

Deri, for his part, doesn’t attack the police from the left but from the right. “Itamar Ben Gvir, wake up,” he declares. “It is unacceptable that what the police did not do in Kaplan against anarchists who sought to destroy the country, they are doing now against citizens crying out that they have been turned into criminals just because they study Torah.” 

The message is clear: street power is legitimate when it belongs to the coalition’s pietists, illegitimate when it belongs to liberal opponents; stun grenades are a tool of justice in Tel Aviv, an outrage in Bnei Brak.

Both camps lean on Kaplan as the gold standard, and each arrives at the opposite conclusion. For Lapid, Haredi roadblocks expose a coalition that weaponizes state power against critics while indulging its own flanks. For Deri, Bnei Brak is proof that police violence was too soft on secular “anarchists” and too hard on “bnei Torah.” 

By the end of the morning, one protester is under arrest, Route 4 is open in both directions, and the only thing truly national is the shared belief that the rule of law now comes with two price lists — one for those who stood on Kaplan, another for those who pray at Geha.
